questions.question: Let $\alpha > 0$. If ${∫}_{0}^{α}\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x + \alpha} - \sqrt{x}}dx = \dfrac{16 + 20\sqrt{2}}{15}$ then $\alpha$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
Given,

${∫}_{0}^{α}\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x + \alpha} - \sqrt{x}}dx = \dfrac{16 + 20\sqrt{2}}{15} . . . . ( 1 )$

Rationalise the denominator in L.H.S we get,

${∫}_{0}^{α}\dfrac{x ( \sqrt{\alpha + x} + \sqrt{x} )}{α}dx = \dfrac{1}{α}\left[{∫}_{0}^{α}x\sqrt{\alpha + x}dx + {∫}_{0}^{α}{x}^{3 / 2}dx\right]$

Put $\alpha + x = {t}^{2} ⇒ dx = 2tdt$

Limit when $x = 0 \to t = \sqrt{\alpha}, x = \alpha \to t = \sqrt{2\alpha}$

$\dfrac{1}{α}{∫}_{\alpha}^{2\alpha}\left({t}^{2} - \alpha\right)2{t}^{2}dt + \dfrac{2{α}^{3 / 2}}{5}$

$= \dfrac{1}{α}{\dfrac{2{t}^{5}}{5} - \dfrac{2\alpha{t}^{3}}{3}}_{\alpha}^{2\alpha} + \dfrac{2{α}^{3 / 2}}{5}$

$= \dfrac{4\alpha\sqrt{2\alpha} + 10\alpha\sqrt{\alpha}}{15}$

From equation $\left(1\right)$

${∫}_{0}^{α}\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x + \alpha} - \sqrt{x}}dx = \dfrac{16 + 20\sqrt{2}}{15}$

$⇒ \dfrac{4\alpha\sqrt{2\alpha} + 10\alpha\sqrt{\alpha}}{15} = \dfrac{16 + 20\sqrt{2}}{15}$

On comparing both sides we get,

$\alpha = 2$

questions.question: $4 \int_0^1\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3+x^2}+\sqrt{1+x^2}}\right) d x-3 \log _e(\sqrt{3})$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} & 4 \int_0^1 \frac{1}{\sqrt{3+\mathrm{x}^2}+\sqrt{1+\mathrm{x}^2}} \mathrm{dx}-3 \ln \sqrt{3} \\ & =4 \int_0^1 \frac{\sqrt{3+\mathrm{x}^2}-\sqrt{1+\mathrm{x}^2}}{\left(3+\mathrm{x}^2\right)-\left(1-\mathrm{x}^2\right)} \mathrm{dx}-\frac{3}{2} \ln 3 \\ & = \\ & 2\left[\left\{\frac{\mathrm{x}}{2} \sqrt{3+\mathrm{x}^2}+\frac{3}{2} \ln \left(\mathrm{x}+\sqrt{3+\mathrm{x}^2}\right)\right\}_0^1\right. \\ & \left.\quad-\left\{\frac{\mathrm{x}}{2} \sqrt{1+\mathrm{x}^2}+\frac{1}{2} \ln \left(\mathrm{x}+\sqrt{1+\mathrm{x}^2}\right)\right\}_0^1\right]-\frac{3}{2} \ln 3\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned}= & 2\left[\left\{\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{4}+\frac{3}{2} \ln (1+\sqrt{4})\right\}-\left\{0+\frac{3}{2} \ln \sqrt{3}\right\}\right. \\ & \left.-\left\{\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{2}+\frac{1}{2} \ln (1+\sqrt{2})\right\}+\left\{0+\frac{1}{2}(0)\right\}\right]-\frac{3}{2} \ln 3\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned} & =2\left[1+\frac{3}{2} \ln 3-\frac{3}{4} \ln 3-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{1}{2} \ln (1+\sqrt{2})\right]-\frac{3}{2} \ln 3 \\ & =2+3 \ln 3-\frac{3}{2} \ln 3-\sqrt{2}-\ln (1+\sqrt{2})-\frac{3}{2} \ln 3 \\ & =2-\sqrt{2}-\ln (1+\sqrt{2})\end{aligned}$

questions.solution:
Rearranging, we get,

${∫}_{\pi / 6}^{\pi / 3}\left(\dfrac{\dfrac{d}{dx}\left({tan}^{4}x\right)}{2} \cdot {sin}^{4}3x + {tan}^{4}x \cdot \dfrac{\dfrac{d}{dx}\left({sin}^{4}3x\right)}{2}\right)dx$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}{∫}_{\pi / 6}^{\pi / 3}\left(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left({tan}^{4}x \cdot {sin}^{4}3x\right)\right)dx$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}{{tan}^{4}x \cdot {sin}^{4}3x}_{\pi / 6}^{\pi / 3}$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\left(\sqrt{3}\right)4 \times 0 - \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)4 \times 1\right]$

$= - \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{9} = - \dfrac{1}{18}$

questions.q: The value of $b > 3$ for which $12{∫}_{3}^{b}\dfrac{1}{\left({x}^{2} - 1\right)\left({x}^{2} - 4\right)}dx = {log}_{e}\left(\dfrac{49}{40}\right)$, is equal to _____.
questions.question: The value of $b > 3$ for which $12{∫}_{3}^{b}\dfrac{1}{\left({x}^{2} - 1\right)\left({x}^{2} - 4\right)}dx = {log}_{e}\left(\dfrac{49}{40}\right)$, is equal to _____.
questions.solution:
Given $12 \times {∫}_{3}^{b}\dfrac{1dx}{\left({x}^{2} - 4\right)\left({x}^{2} - 1\right)} = ln\left[\dfrac{49}{40}\right] \text{ and } 4b > 3$

$⇒$ By Using partial fraction

$\dfrac{1}{\left({x}^{2} - 4\right)\left({x}^{2} - 1\right)} = \dfrac{1}{3}\left(\dfrac{1}{{x}^{2} - 4} - \dfrac{1}{{x}^{2} - 1}\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{12}{3}{∫}_{3}^{b}\left[\dfrac{1}{{x}^{2} - 4} - \dfrac{1}{{x}^{2} - 1}\right] = ln\left(\dfrac{49}{40}\right)$

$⇒ 4{\dfrac{1}{4}log\left(\dfrac{x - 2}{x + 2}\right) - \dfrac{1}{2}log\left(\dfrac{x - 1}{x + 1}\right)}_{3}^{b} = ln\left(\dfrac{49}{40}\right)$

$⇒ log\left(\dfrac{\left(b - 2\right)\left(b + 1\right)2}{\left(b + 2\right)\left(b - 1\right)2} \times \dfrac{5}{4}\right) = log\dfrac{49}{40}$

$⇒ \dfrac{\left(b - 2\right)\left(b + 1\right)2}{\left(b + 2\right)\left(b - 1\right)2} \times \dfrac{5}{4} = \dfrac{49}{40}$

$⇒ \dfrac{\left(b - 2\right)\left(b + 1\right)2}{\left(b + 2\right)\left(b - 1\right)2} = \dfrac{49}{50} . . . \left(i\right)$

Comparing by hit and trial and taking $\left(b + 1\right)2 = 49 ⇒ b + 1 = 7 ⇒ b = 6$

Now putting $b = 6$ in equation (i) to corsscheck,

we get $\dfrac{4 \times {7}^{2}}{8 \times {5}^{2}} = \dfrac{49}{50}$ which is true

So $b = 6$ is correct option,

Hence $b = 6$
questions.explanation:

questions.question: The value of ${∫}_{\pi3}^{\pi2}\left(2 + 3sinx\right)sinx\left(1 + cosx\right)dx$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Let, $I = {∫}_{\pi3}^{\pi2}\dfrac{2 + 3sinx}{sinx\left(1 + cosx\right)}dx$

Now rearranging the above integral we get,

$I = {∫}_{\pi3}^{\pi2}\dfrac{2}{sinx\left(1 + cosx\right)}dx + {∫}_{\pi3}^{\pi2}3\left(1 + cosx\right)dx$

$⇒ I = {∫}_{\pi3}^{\pi2}\dfrac{2sinx}{{sin}^{2}x\left(1 + cosx\right)}dx + {∫}_{\pi3}^{\pi2}3\left(2{cos}^{2}\dfrac{x}{2}\right)dx$

$⇒ I = \mathop{{∫}_{\pi3}^{\pi2}\dfrac{2sinx}{{sin}^{2}x\left(1 + cosx\right)} d x ⏟}_{I1} + \dfrac{3}{2}\mathop{{∫}_{\pi3}^{\pi2}{sec}^{2}\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) d x ⏟}_{I2}$

$⇒ I = \mathop{{∫}_{\pi3}^{\pi2}\dfrac{2sinx}{{sin}^{2}x\left(1 + cosx\right)}dx ⏟}_{I1} + \dfrac{3}{2} \times 2\mathop{{tan\dfrac{x}{2}}_{\pi3}^{\pi2} ⏟}_{I2}$

$⇒ I = \mathop{{∫}_{\pi3}^{\pi2}\dfrac{2sinx}{{sin}^{2}x\left(1 + cosx\right)}dx ⏟}_{I1} + 3\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{3}\right)$

Now solving ${I}_{1}$ we get,

${I}_{1} = {∫}_{\pi3}^{\pi2}\dfrac{2sinx}{{sin}^{2}x\left(1 + cosx\right)}dx$

$⇒ {I}_{1} = 2{∫}_{\pi3}^{\pi2}\dfrac{1}{sinx\left(1 + cosx\right)}dx$

$⇒ {I}_{1} = 2{∫}_{\pi3}^{\pi2}\dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{2tan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)}{1 + {tan}^{2}\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)}\right)\left(1 + \dfrac{1 - tan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)}{1 + {tan}^{2}\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)}\right)}dx$

$⇒ {I}_{1} = \dfrac{1}{2}{∫}_{\pi3}^{\pi2}\dfrac{\left[1 + {tan}^{2}\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\right]{sec}^{2}\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)}{tan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)}dx$

Put $tan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) = v ⇒ \dfrac{1}{2}{sec}^{2}\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)dx = dv$

$⇒ {I}_{1} = {∫}_{1\sqrt{3}}^{1}\dfrac{\left(1 + {v}^{2}\right)dv}{v}$

$⇒ {I}_{1} = {{log}_{e}\left(v\right) + \dfrac{v2}{2}}_{1\sqrt{3}}^{1}$

$⇒ {I}_{1} = {log}_{e}\left(1\right) - {log}_{e}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{3}\right)$

$⇒ {I}_{1} = {log}_{e}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) + \dfrac{1}{3}$

So,

$I = \dfrac{1}{3} + {log}_{e}\sqrt{3} + 3\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{3}\right)$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{10}{3} - \sqrt{3} + {log}_{e}\sqrt{3}$

questions.question: For $0 < a < 1$, the value of the integral ${∫}_{0}^{π}\dfrac{dx}{1 - 2acosx + {a}^{2}}$ is :
questions.solution:
Given: $I = {∫}_{0}^{π}\dfrac{dx}{1 - 2acosx + {a}^{2}} . . . \left(i\right)$

$⇒ I = {∫}_{0}^{π}\dfrac{dx}{1 - 2acos\left(\pi - x\right) + {a}^{2}}$

$⇒ I = {∫}_{0}^{π}\dfrac{dx}{1 + 2acosx + {a}^{2}} . . . \left(ii\right)$

Adding $\left(i\right)$ and $\left(ii\right)$,

$⇒ 2I = {∫}_{0}^{π}\dfrac{dx}{1 - 2acosx + {a}^{2}} + {∫}_{0}^{π}\dfrac{dx}{1 + 2acosx + {a}^{2}}$

$⇒ 2I = {∫}_{0}^{π}\left(\dfrac{1}{1 - 2acosx + {a}^{2}} + \dfrac{1}{1 + 2acosx + {a}^{2}}\right)dx$

$⇒ 2I = {∫}_{0}^{π}\left(\dfrac{1 + 2acosx + {a}^{2} + 1 - 2acosx + {a}^{2}}{\left(1 + {a}^{2}\right)2 - \left(2acosx\right)2}\right)dx$

$⇒ 2I = {∫}_{0}^{π}\left(\dfrac{2\left(1 + {a}^{2}\right)}{\left(1 + {a}^{2}\right)2 - \left(2acosx\right)2}\right)dx$

$⇒ 2I = 2{∫}_{0}^{\pi2}\dfrac{2\left(1 + {a}^{2}\right)}{\left(1 + {a}^{2}\right)2 - 4{a}^{2}{cos}^{2}x}dx$

$⇒ I = {∫}_{0}^{\pi2}\dfrac{2\left(1 + {a}^{2}\right) \cdot {sec}^{2}x}{\left(1 + {a}^{2}\right)2 \cdot {sec}^{2}x - 4{a}^{2}}dx$

$⇒ I = {∫}_{0}^{\pi2}\dfrac{2\left(1 + {a}^{2}\right) \cdot {sec}^{2}x}{\left(1 + {a}^{2}\right)2 + \left(1 + {a}^{2}\right)2{tan}^{2}x - 4{a}^{2}}dx$

$⇒ I = {∫}_{0}^{\pi2}\dfrac{2\left(1 + {a}^{2}\right) \cdot {sec}^{2}x}{\left(1 + {a}^{2} - 2a\right)2 + \left(1 + {a}^{2}\right)2{tan}^{2}x}dx$

$⇒ I = {∫}_{0}^{\pi2}\dfrac{2 \cdot \left(1 + {a}^{2}\right) \cdot {sec}^{2}x}{\left(1 + {a}^{2}\right)2 \cdot {tan}^{2}x + \left(1 - {a}^{2}\right)2}dx$

$⇒ I = {∫}_{0}^{\pi2}\dfrac{\dfrac{2 \cdot {sec}^{2}x}{1 + {a}^{2}} \cdot dx}{{tan}^{2}x + \left(\dfrac{1 - {a}^{2}}{1 + {a}^{2}}\right)2}$

Let, $tanx = t$

$⇒ {sec}^{2}xdx = dt$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{2}{1 + {a}^{2}}{∫}_{0}^{∞}\dfrac{dt}{{t}^{2} + \left(\dfrac{1 - {a}^{2}}{1 + {a}^{2}}\right)2}$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{2}{1 + {a}^{2}} \times 1\left(\dfrac{1 - {a}^{2}}{1 + {a}^{2}}\right){{tan}^{- 1}t\left(\dfrac{1 - {a}^{2}}{1 + {a}^{2}}\right)}_{0}^{∞}$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{2}{1 - {a}^{2}}\left[{tan}^{- 1}\left(\infty\right) - {tan}^{- 1}\left(0\right)\right]$

questions.question: Let $(2^{1-a} + 2^{1+a})$, $f(a)$, $(3^a + 3^{-a})$ be in A.P. and $\alpha$ be the minimum value of $f(a)$. Then the value of the integral $\int_{\log_e(\alpha-1)}^{\log_e(\alpha)} \dfrac{dx}{(e^{2x} - e^{-2x})}$ is :
questions.solution:
Since $(2^{1-a} + 2^{1+a})$, $f(a)$, and $(3^a + 3^{-a})$ are in A.P., we have:

$2f(a) = 2^{1-a} + 2^{1+a} + 3^a + 3^{-a}$

$f(a) = (2^{-a} + 2^a) + \dfrac{1}{2}(3^a + 3^{-a})$

Using the AM-GM inequality, $x + \dfrac{1}{x} \ge 2$ for $x > 0$.

$2^a + 2^{-a} \ge 2$ and $3^a + 3^{-a} \ge 2$.

The minimum value of $f(a)$ occurs when $a = 0$.

$\alpha = f(0) = (2^0 + 2^0) + \dfrac{1}{2}(3^0 + 3^0) = 2 + 1 = 3$.

Now, we evaluate the integral:

$I = \int_{\log_e 2}^{\log_e 3} \dfrac{dx}{e^{2x} - e^{-2x}} = \int_{\log_e 2}^{\log_e 3} \dfrac{e^{2x}}{e^{4x} - 1} dx$

Let $e^{2x} = t \Rightarrow 2e^{2x} dx = dt$.

When $x = \log_e 2$, $t = e^{2\log_e 2} = 4$.

When $x = \log_e 3$, $t = e^{2\log_e 3} = 9$.

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{4}^{9} \dfrac{dt}{t^2 - 1}$

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \left[ \dfrac{1}{2} \log_e \left| \dfrac{t-1}{t+1} \right| \right]_{4}^{9}$

$I = \dfrac{1}{4} \left( \log_e \dfrac{8}{10} - \log_e \dfrac{3}{5} \right)$

$I = \dfrac{1}{4} \left( \log_e \dfrac{4}{5} - \log_e \dfrac{3}{5} \right) = \dfrac{1}{4} \log_e \left( \dfrac{4/5}{3/5} \right) = \dfrac{1}{4} \log_e \left( \dfrac{4}{3} \right)$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{4} \log_e\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)$

questions.question: The value of $\int_{-\pi / 6}^{\pi / 6}\left(\frac{\pi+4 x^{11}}{1-\sin (|x|+\pi / 6)}\right) d x$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
Split: $\int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6} \frac{\pi}{1 - \sin(|x| + \pi/6)} dx + \int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6} \frac{4x^{11}}{1 - \sin(|x| + \pi/6)} dx$.

$\frac{1}{1-\sin u} = \sec^2 u + \sec u \tan u$.
$= 2\pi [\tan u + \sec u]_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} = 2\pi[(\sqrt{3}+2) - \sqrt{3}] = 4\pi$.

Applying ${∫}_{a}^{b}f\left(x\right) d x = {∫}_{a}^{b}f\left(a + b - x\right) d x$ rule we get,

$⇒ I = \mathop{∫}_{- \dfrac{π}{2}}^{\pi2}\dfrac{8\sqrt{2}cosx\left({e}^{sinx}\right)}{\left(1 + {e}^{sinx}\right)\left(1 + {sin}^{4}x\right)}dx . . . \left(ii\right)$

Adding $\left(i\right)\text{and}\left(ii\right)$

$⇒ 2I = \mathop{∫}_{- \dfrac{π}{2}}^{\pi2}\dfrac{8\sqrt{2}cosx}{1 + {sin}^{4}x}dx$

$⇒ I = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{\pi2}\dfrac{8\sqrt{2}cosx}{1 + {sin}^{4}x}dx$

Putting, $sinx = t$

$⇒ I = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{1}\dfrac{8\sqrt{2}}{1 + {t}^{4}}dx$

$⇒ I = 4\sqrt{2}\mathop{∫}_{0}^{1}\left(\dfrac{1 + \dfrac{1}{t2}}{{t}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{t2}} - \dfrac{1 - \dfrac{1}{t2}}{{t}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{t2}}\right)dt$

$⇒ I = 4\sqrt{2}\mathop{∫}_{0}^{1}\left(\dfrac{1 + \dfrac{1}{t2}}{\left(t - \dfrac{1}{t}\right)2 + 2} - \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{t2}\right)\left(t + \dfrac{1}{t}\right)2 - 2\right)dt$

$⇒ \alpha = 2$ and $\beta = 2$

$⇒ I = 2\pi\mathop{{∫}_{0}^{\pi2}\dfrac{x \cdot sinxcosx}{{sin}^{4}x + {cos}^{4}x} d x ⏟}_{I1} - {π}^{2}{∫}_{0}^{\pi2}\dfrac{sinxcosx}{{sin}^{4}x + {cos}^{4}x} d x$

Now, solving ${I}_{1} = {∫}_{0}^{\pi2}\dfrac{x \cdot sinxcosx}{{sin}^{4}x + {cos}^{4}x}dx . . . . \left(1\right)$

$f ( - x ) = - f ( x ) ⇒ f$ is also odd.

$I = {∫}_{- \dfrac{π}{2}}^{\pi2}\left(f ( x ) + \dfrac{{x}^{2}cosx}{1 + {e}^{x}}\right)dx . . . \left(i\right)$

Zeros in $[0, \pi]$: $x = 0, \pi/2, 2\pi/3, \pi$

$6 \times \frac{17}{6} = 17$

questions.question: Let $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2} (|\sin x| + [x \sin x])\,dx = 2(3 - \cos 2) + \beta$, where $[\cdot]$ is the greatest integer function. Then $\beta \sin\left(\dfrac{\beta}{2}\right)$ equals:
questions.solution:
Let $I = \displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2} \left(|\sin x| + [x \sin x]\right) dx = I_1 + I_2$, where
$I_1 = \displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2} |\sin x|\, dx$ and $I_2 = \displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2} [x \sin x]\, dx$.

Evaluating $I_1$:
Since $|\sin x|$ is even, $I_1 = 2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} |\sin x|\, dx$.
For $x \in [0, 2]$, $2 < \pi$, so $\sin x \geq 0$ and $|\sin x| = \sin x$.
$I_1 = 2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} \sin x\, dx = 2\left[-\cos x\right]_0^2 = 2(1 - \cos 2) = 2 - 2\cos 2$

Evaluating $I_2$:
Let $g(x) = x\sin x$. Then $g(-x) = (-x)\sin(-x) = x\sin x = g(x)$, so $g(x)$ is even, and hence $[x\sin x]$ is also even.
$I_2 = 2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} [x\sin x]\, dx$

Behaviour of $y = x\sin x$ on $[0, 2]$:
At $x = 0$, $y = 0$. At $x = 2$, $y = 2\sin 2 \approx 1.818$.
$y' = \sin x + x\cos x > 0$ on $[0, 2]$, so $y$ is strictly increasing on this interval.

Therefore, $x\sin x$ takes each value in $[0, 1.818]$ exactly once, and crosses $1$ at some unique $\alpha \in (0, 2)$ with $\alpha\sin\alpha = 1$.

For $x \in [0, \alpha)$: $0 \leq x\sin x < 1 \Rightarrow [x\sin x] = 0$
For $x \in [\alpha, 2]$: $1 \leq x\sin x < 2 \Rightarrow [x\sin x] = 1$

$I_2 = 2\left(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\alpha} 0\, dx + \displaystyle\int_{\alpha}^{2} 1\, dx\right) = 2(2 - \alpha) = 4 - 2\alpha$

Combining:
$I = I_1 + I_2 = (2 - 2\cos 2) + (4 - 2\alpha) = 6 - 2\cos 2 - 2\alpha$

Given $I = 2(3 - \cos 2) + \beta = 6 - 2\cos 2 + \beta$, so:
$6 - 2\cos 2 - 2\alpha = 6 - 2\cos 2 + \beta \Rightarrow \beta = -2\alpha$

Now:
$\beta \sin\left(\dfrac{\beta}{2}\right) = -2\alpha \sin\left(\dfrac{-2\alpha}{2}\right) = -2\alpha \sin(-\alpha) = 2\alpha\sin\alpha$

Since $\alpha\sin\alpha = 1$:
$\beta \sin\left(\dfrac{\beta}{2}\right) = 2 \cdot 1 = 2$

Hence, the correct option is $(2)\ 2$.

questions.question: Let a differentiable function $f$ satisfy the equation $\int_{0}^{36} f\left(\frac{t x}{36}\right) d t=4 \alpha f(x)$. If $y=f(x)$ is a standard parabola passing through the points $(2,1)$ and $(-4, \beta)$, then $\beta^{\alpha}$ is equal to $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution:
From $\int_0^{36} f\left(\frac{tx}{36}\right) dt = 4\alpha f(x)$, substitute $u = \frac{tx}{36}$ to get $\frac{36}{x} \int_0^x f(u) du = 4\alpha f(x)$.
Differentiating: $f(x) = \frac{\alpha}{9}[f(x) + xf'(x)]$, which simplifies to $(9-\alpha)f(x) = \alpha x f'(x)$.
This gives $\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)} = \frac{9-\alpha}{\alpha x}$, integrating to $f(x) = Kx^{\frac{9-\alpha}{\alpha}}$.
For f to be a standard parabola: $\frac{9-\alpha}{\alpha} = 2 \Rightarrow \alpha = 3$.
Thus $f(x) = Kx^2$. Using point $(2,1)$: $K = \frac{1}{4}$, so $f(x) = \frac{x^2}{4}$.
At $(-4, \beta)$: $\beta = \frac{16}{4} = 4$.
Therefore $\beta^\alpha = 4^3 = 64$

questions.question: Let \(f:(0, \infty) \rightarrow \mathbf{R}\) be a twice differentiable function. If for some \(\mathrm{a} \neq 0, \int_0^1 f(\lambda x) \mathrm{d} \lambda=\mathrm{a} f(x), f(1)=1\) and \(f(16)=\frac{1}{8}\), then \(16-f^{\prime}\left(\frac{1}{16}\right)\) is equal to _______.
questions.solution:
Given, $\int_0^1 f(\lambda x) d \lambda=a f(x)$
Let $\lambda x=u$
$d \lambda=\frac{1}{x} d u$
$\therefore$ From (1) $\frac{1}{x} \int_0^x f(u) d u=a f(x)$
$\Rightarrow \int_0^x f(u) d u=\operatorname{axf}(x)$
Differentiate both sides
$\begin{aligned}
& f(x)=a\left(x f^{\prime}(x)+f(x)\right) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad f(x)=a x f^{\prime}(x)+a f(x) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad(1-a) f(x)=a x f^{\prime}(x) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x)}=\frac{(1-a)}{a} \cdot \frac{1}{x}
\end{aligned}$
Integrate both side w.r.t. ( $x$ )
$\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \quad \int \frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x)} d x=\frac{(1-a)}{a} \int \frac{1}{x} d x \\
& \Rightarrow \ln f(x)=\left(\frac{1-a}{a}\right) \ln x+c
\end{aligned}$
Now at $x=1 f(1)=1$
$\Rightarrow c=0$
Also given $f(16)=\frac{1}{8}$
$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \quad \frac{1}{8}=(16)^{\frac{1-a}{a}} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 2^{-3}=2^{\frac{4-4 a}{a}} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad-3=\frac{4-4 a}{a} \\
& \Rightarrow-3 a=4-4 a \\
& \Rightarrow a=4 \\
& \therefore \quad f(x)=x^{-3 / 4} \\
& f(x)=\frac{-3}{4} x^{-\frac{7}{4}}
\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned} & \text { Put } x=\frac{1}{16} \\ & f^{\prime}\left(\frac{1}{16}\right)=\frac{-3}{4}\left(\frac{1}{16}\right)^{-7 / 4}=\frac{-3}{4} \cdot 2^{-4 x\left(\frac{-7}{4}\right)}=-96 \\ & \therefore \quad 16-f^{\prime}\left(\frac{1}{16}\right) \Rightarrow 16-(-96)=112\end{aligned}$

questions.question: If $f(x)$ satisfies the relation $f(x)=e^{x}+\int_{0}^{1}\left(y+x e^{x}\right) f(y) d y$, then $e+f(0)$ is equal to $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution:
$f(x) = e^x + \displaystyle\int_0^1 (y + xe^x)f(y)\, dy$

Splitting the integral:
$f(x) = e^x + \displaystyle\int_0^1 yf(y)\, dy + xe^x \int_0^1 f(y)\, dy$

Let $A = \displaystyle\int_0^1 yf(y)\, dy$ and $B = \displaystyle\int_0^1 f(y)\, dy$

$\Rightarrow f(x) = (1 + Bx)e^x + A$

At $x = 0$: $f(0) = 1 + A$

Now compute $B$ using the expression for $f(y)$:
$B = \displaystyle\int_0^1 \left[(1 + By)e^y + A\right] dy$
$B = \displaystyle\int_0^1 e^y\, dy + B\int_0^1 ye^y\, dy + \int_0^1 A\, dy$

Evaluating each integral:
$\displaystyle\int_0^1 e^y\, dy = e - 1$
$\displaystyle\int_0^1 ye^y\, dy = [ye^y]_0^1 - \int_0^1 e^y\, dy = e - (e - 1) = 1$
$\displaystyle\int_0^1 A\, dy = A$

$\Rightarrow B = (e - 1) + B(1) + A$
$\Rightarrow 0 = e - 1 + A$
$\Rightarrow A = 1 - e$

$f(0) = 1 + A = 1 + (1 - e) = 2 - e$

$e + f(0) = e + (2 - e) = 2$

Answer: $2$

And,$f\left(x\right) = x + \dfrac{a}{{π}^{2} - 4}sinx + \dfrac{b}{{π}^{2} - 4}cosx, x \in \mathbb{R}$

$⇒ \dfrac{b}{{π}^{2} - 4} = {∫}_{0}^{\pi / 2}sinyf\left(y\right)dy \ldots \left(2\right)$

Adding equation $\left(1\right)$ and equation $\left(2\right)$ we get,

$∵ {∫}_{0}^{a}f ( x ) d x = {∫}_{0}^{a}f ( a - x ) d x$

$∴ \dfrac{a + b}{{π}^{2} - 4} = {∫}_{0}^{\pi / 2}\left(siny + cosy\right)f\left(\dfrac{π}{2} - y\right)dy \ldots \left(4\right)$

$⇒ \left(a + b\right) = - 2\pi\left(\pi + 2\right)$

questions.question: Let $f$ be a twice differentiable function on $R$. If ${f}^{'}\left(0\right) = 4$ and $f\left(x\right) + {∫}_{0}^{x}\left(x - t\right){f}^{'}\left(t\right)dt$ $= \left({e}^{2x} + {e}^{- 2x}\right)cos2x + \dfrac{2}{a}x$, then $\left(2a + 1\right)5{a}^{2}$ is equal to _______.
questions.solution:
Given,

$f\left(x\right) + {∫}_{0}^{x}\left(x - t\right){f}^{'}\left(t\right)dt = \left({e}^{2x} + {e}^{- 2x}\right)cos2x + \dfrac{2x}{a} ⋯ \left(i\right)$

Putting $x = 0$ both side we get, $f\left(0\right) = 2 ⋯ \left(ii\right)$

On differentiating equation $\left(i\right)$ w.r.t. $x$ we get:

${f}^{'}\left(x\right) + {∫}_{0}^{x}{f}^{'}\left(t\right)dt + x{f}^{'}\left(x\right) - x{f}^{'}\left(x\right) = 2\left({e}^{2x} - {e}^{- 2x}\right)cos2x - 2\left({e}^{2x} + {e}^{- 2x}\right)sin2x + \dfrac{2}{a}$

$⇒ {f}^{'}\left(x\right) + f\left(x\right) - f\left(0\right) = 2\left({e}^{2x} - {e}^{- 2x}\right)cos2x - 2\left({e}^{2x} + {e}^{- 2x}\right)sin2x + \dfrac{2}{a}$

Replace $x$ by $0$ we get:

$⇒ 4 = \dfrac{2}{a} ⇒ a = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Now putting the value of $a$ in$\left(2a + 1\right)5 \cdot {a}^{2}$

We get, ${2}^{5} \cdot \dfrac{1}{22} = {2}^{3} = 8$

questions.solution:
Given, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{n}\dfrac{n3}{\left({n}^{2} + {k}^{2}\right)\left({n}^{2} + 3{k}^{2}\right)}$

$= \lim_{n \to \infty}\dfrac{1}{n}\mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{n}\dfrac{1}{\left(1 + \dfrac{k2}{n2}\right)\left(1 + 3 \cdot \dfrac{k2}{n2}\right)}$

Now, using limit as a sum integral we get,

$= {∫}_{0}^{1}\dfrac{dx}{\left(1 + {x}^{2}\right)\left(1 + 3{x}^{2}\right)}$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[{∫}_{0}^{1}3\left(1 + 3{x}^{2}\right) - 1\left(1 + {x}^{2}\right)\right]dx$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[{∫}_{0}^{1}1\left(\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)2 + {x}^{2}\right) - 1\left(1 + {x}^{2}\right)\right]dx$

$= \dfrac{13\pi}{8 \cdot ( 4\sqrt{3} + 3 )}$

questions.solution:
Using $u = x - t$: $\int_0^x t^2 \sin(x-t)\,dt = \int_0^x (x-u)^2 \sin u\,du$.
Expanding and integrating term by term:
$= x^2(1-\cos x) - 2x(-x\cos x + \sin x) + (-x^2\cos x + 2x\sin x + 2\cos x - 2)$
$= x^2 + 2\cos x - 2$.
Setting equal to $x^2$: $2\cos x - 2 = 0 \Rightarrow \cos x = 1 \Rightarrow x = 2n\pi$.
In $[0, 100]$: $2n\pi \le 100 \Rightarrow n \le \frac{50}{\pi} \approx 15.9$.
So $n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, 15$, giving $16$ elements.

questions.question: The value of $k \in \mathrm{N}$ for which the integral $I_n=\int_0^1\left(1-x^k\right)^n d x, n \in \mathbb{N}$, satisfies $147 I_{20}=148 I_{21}$ is
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & I_n=\int_0^1\left(1-x^k\right)^n \cdot 1 d x \\ & I_n=\left(1-x^k\right)^n \cdot x-n k \int_0^1\left(1-x^k\right)^{n-1} \cdot x^{k-1} \cdot d x \\ & I_n=n k \int_0^1\left[\left(1-x^k\right)^n-\left(1-x^k\right)^{n-1}\right] d x \\ & I_n=n k I_n-n k I_n \\ & \frac{I_n}{I_{n-1}}=\frac{n k}{n k+1} \\ & \frac{I_{21}}{I_{20}}=\frac{21 k}{1+21 k} \\ & =\frac{147}{148} \Rightarrow k=7\end{aligned}$
